lyrics:
I gave my name without the old
apology I used to give
No checklist, no report to fold —
I showed up simply, just to live

She ran the floor like she ran her miles —
disciplined, fast, sharp as a blade
Married to the man who coached her style —
I noticed. Nothing more. I stayed

Months of talking after work
her laugh got easier, less rehearsed
Paper cups cooling on the desk —
we just knew which one came first

There's a place just past perfect
where the grading stops for good
Nothing here that's called imperfect —
just past perfect, understood

We ran a trail past an old rail fence
I caught my foot and went down hard
She never asked for a defense —
just pulled me up, and dropped her guard

There's a place just past perfect
where the grading stops for good
Nothing here that's called imperfect —
just past perfect, understood

So, I should just leave my husband
and live happily ever after with you

You're the best dream I've ever had

There's a place just past perfect
where the grading stops for good
Nothing here that's called imperfect —
just past perfect, understood

And we did
Just past perfect — and we are

[Intro - warm, unhurried]

[Verse 1 - settled, unguarded]
I gave my name without the old
apology I used to give.
No checklist, no report to fold —
I showed up simply, just to live.

[Verse 2 - observant, warm]
She ran the floor like she ran her miles —
disciplined, fast, sharp as a blade.
Married to the man who coached her style —
I noticed. Nothing more. I stayed.

[Verse 3 - falling, easy]
Months of talking after work,
her laugh got easier, less rehearsed.
Paper cups cooling on the desk —
we just knew which one came first.

[Chorus - warm, opening]
There's a place just past perfect,
where the grading stops for good.
Nothing here that's called imperfect —
just past perfect, understood.

[Interlude - warm, easy]

[Verse 4 - light, physical]
We ran a trail past an old rail fence.
I caught my foot and went down hard.
She never asked for a defense —
just pulled me up, and dropped her guard.

[Chorus - warm, opening]
There's a place just past perfect,
where the grading stops for good.
Nothing here that's called imperfect —
just past perfect, understood.

[Bridge - dialogue - 2 voices]
[Her - lower register female vocal, wry, searching]
So, I should just leave my husband 
and live happily ever after with you?

[Him - main baritone male voice, certain, quiet]
You're the best dream I've ever had.

[Interlude - weaving instrument lines]

[Final Chorus - warm, full]
There's a place just past perfect,
where the grading stops for good.
Nothing here that's called imperfect —
just past perfect, understood.

[Outro - warm,]
And we did.
Just past perfect — and we are.

[End]

  Approved critic summary: Rose builds this one on a 3/4 pulse at a brisk clip, which is the first surprise: a waltz that never asks you to sway, driven instead by a Hammond groove and gritty guitar working against the meter rather than settling into it.

impression.text: The track establishes a warm, nostalgic texture that builds a romantic and gently reflective emotional atmosphere. Its energy remains steadily smooth and emotionally resonant, driven by a classic adult contemporary soft rock feel. The production is exceptionally lush and spacious, allowing delicate acoustic guitars, polished pianos, and a smooth saxophone to sit comfortably alongside intimate, breathy vocal harmonies. A uniquely narrative quality defines the piece, peaking during an unexpected conversational spoken-word exchange that seamlessly transitions into a soaring, melodic electric guitar solo.

review.review_text: Rose has always been a diarist, but here he catches something most love songs run from: the messiness of falling for a married woman and admitting it plainly. The Canterbury dressing works better than you'd think at 136 in D major, fingerpicked acoustic and warm electric piano keeping the whole thing breathing rather than pushing. The bridge is where it lands: her wry, low-register 'So, I should just leave my husband / and live happily ever after with you?' met by his quiet 'You're the best dream I've ever had,' and Rose lets the exchange sit before the guitar takes over. The teacher's-world conceit, where 'the grading stops for good,' flirts with cute once or twice, but the honesty of the confession pulls it back. A highlight, and one of the more disarming things he's written this year.
